articles.title_orig: Samsung W27 Foldable: 200MP, $2,650 in China [2026]
articles.title_zh: Samsung W27 Foldable: 200MP, $2,650 in China [2026]
articles.content_orig:
Samsung has put a gold-trimmed foldable on sale in China, and the Samsung W27 is the most expensive way yet to buy the company’s current book-style flagship. According to NewsBricks, GSMArena and 9to5Google, the W27 launched on October 29, 2026, with a 200MP main camera, an 8-inch inner screen and a starting price of CNY 18,999, roughly $2,800 to $2,850. The 1TB version costs CNY 21,999, or about $3,300.
The phone is not a new design. It is a dressed-up, China-only edition of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, with a fixed 16GB of RAM, two lacquer-style colors and gold plating on the frame, hinge and camera rings. Buyers also get a Kevlar case and a gift-box presentation. Samsung is selling status here, and the spec sheet is nearly identical to the standard model. For readers tracking the 200MP race, our look at the Motorola Signature 27 launch covers a rival that bets on zoom instead of gold.
This analysis walks through what Samsung announced, what the numbers say about the price premium, how the W27 compares with the phone it is built on, and what the launch tells us about the luxury foldable market. It sits in our hardware coverage because the story is mostly about silicon, glass and metal, and about how much a finish is worth to a buyer. Every figure below comes from the outlets named in the text. Where reports disagree or stay silent, we say so.

Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.
The W27 arrived as part of a series Samsung markets under the Heart to the World name in China. GSMArena reported that the phone went official on October 29, 2026, and that it is sold through Samsung’s Chinese online store. NewsBricks, which flagged the launch as one of the day’s top trending technology stories, reported that general sales begin on November 13, 2026. The two dates are not in conflict. One marks the announcement and the opening of the store listing, and the other marks the date when the phone begins to ship in volume.
Both outlets agree on the pricing structure. The phone comes in a single memory configuration with 16GB of RAM and two storage tiers, 512GB and 1TB. The cheaper model costs CNY 18,999. The larger one costs CNY 21,999. NewsBricks and GSMArena converted those figures to about $2,850 and $3,300, while 9to5Google rounded the entry price to around $2,800. The small gap comes from exchange-rate rounding, so the safest summary is a range of $2,800 to $2,850 for the base model.
Samsung did not frame the W27 as a technology leap. The company framed it as a collector’s object. The package includes a Kevlar magnetic case, a charger and a USB cable, according to TechGenyz and 9to5Google. NewsBricks added that the box itself uses dual-swing doors, a detail that tells you who the marketing is aimed at. A buyer comparing spec sheets would not care about the packaging. A buyer giving a phone as a gift or a status symbol cares a lot.
The table below collects the specifications that two or more outlets reported consistently. Items that only one outlet mentioned are called out in the sections that follow instead of the table, so the numbers here carry the most weight.
Two details stand out. First, the chipset is the Galaxy-tuned version of Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, the same silicon that 9to5Google says the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra uses. Second, the RAM is fixed. 9to5Google noted that 16GB is standard on the W27 no matter which storage tier you choose, which simplifies the lineup into two SKUs.
The headline feature in nearly every report is the 200MP main sensor. Sammy Fans, NewsBricks and TechGenyz also list a 50MP ultrawide camera and a 10MP telephoto lens with 3x optical zoom. TechGenyz added that the main lens opens to f/1.7, offers 2x adaptive zoom and records 8K video. Those extra points came from a single outlet, so treat them as reported rather than confirmed by Samsung’s own spec page.
A 200MP sensor on a foldable matters for two reasons. It lets the camera crop into the frame and still deliver a usable image, which gives the phone a form of lossless digital zoom around its 2x mark. It also helps close a long-standing gap between foldables and slab phones, where the thin hinge-limited body has historically forced compromises in camera depth. Putting one in a folding body suggests Samsung now treats the Fold line as a true flagship rather than a niche device, though that reading is ours and not a Samsung statement.
The selfie hardware is symmetrical. TechGenyz and Sammy Fans both report a 10MP front camera on the cover screen and another on the inner screen. That is a modest sensor by current standards, and it is the one place where the W27 does not try to impress on paper. Buyers who want a stronger front camera usually use the rear system with the cover display as a viewfinder, a trick every large foldable supports.
The inner screen measures 8.0 inches, which makes the W27 a tablet-class foldable when open. The outer panel measures 6.5 inches. NewsBricks reports that both displays are LTPO AMOLED panels with a 120Hz refresh rate and a peak brightness of 3,000 nits. TechGenyz put the inner display at 422 pixels per inch and called it a second-generation Dynamic AMOLED. GSMArena reports that both panels are protected by Corning Gorilla Glass Ceramic 3.
Sammy Fans lists the weight at 215 grams, the folded thickness at 8.9 mm and the dust and water rating at IP48. TechGenyz agrees on the weight and folded thickness and adds an unfolded thickness of 4.1 mm. The IP48 rating deserves a short explanation. The first digit covers dust, and the 4 means protection against solid objects larger than 1 mm. The second digit covers water, and the 8 means the phone survives immersion. In practice, foldables with this rating resist submersion but not fine dust, so a beach trip remains a risk.
NewsBricks says the gold plating covers an aluminum mid-frame, the hinges and the camera rings. Plating on a hinge is more than decoration. It is a surface that gets touched and flexed thousands of times, so the finish has to survive wear. Sammy Fans described the frame and camera island as having a special textured finish. Samsung has not published a durability figure for the gold coating, and none of the reports we reviewed include one. Early owners will tell us how it ages.
The Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy is the top mobile platform in Samsung’s current lineup. Pairing it with 16GB of RAM gives the W27 enough headroom for multi-window work on the 8-inch screen, where two or three apps often run side by side. With only two storage options, Samsung avoids the confusion of a configuration matrix and makes the price ladder easy to read: CNY 18,999 for 512GB and CNY 21,999 for 1TB.
The battery is the least exciting number on the sheet. GSMArena, NewsBricks and TechGenyz all report 5,000mAh with 45W wired charging. NewsBricks mentions 20W wireless charging and describes the cell as a dual battery, which is how most foldables split capacity across the two halves. TechGenyz cites a claimed video playback time of about 27 hours under lab conditions. Lab claims are rarely matched in daily use, so independent tests will be the real measure. For context on what a very large cell can do, our review of the Oppo Find X10 and its 25-hour battery result shows how much further slab phones have pushed endurance.
Foldables have always traded battery for thinness, and the W27 follows that pattern. A 5,000mAh pack is a respectable capacity for a device that folds to 8.9 mm. A luxury buyer who values daily endurance may notice the modest capacity, though the W27’s target audience likely cares more about presentation than about milliamp-hours.
Price is the loudest part of this launch. At CNY 18,999, the entry model is a serious outlay, and the 1TB model costs roughly $450 more at the converted rate. The step between tiers, CNY 3,000, is about 15.8 percent of the base price. The table below shows the conv

articles.title_orig: US jails two Chinese nationals for spying
articles.title_zh: US jails two Chinese nationals for spying
articles.content_orig:
Two Chinese nationals have been jailed in the United States after admitting to trying to recruit US military service members to spy for Beijing.
Liren “Ryan” Lai, 40, and Yuance Chen, 39, were each sentenced to 30 months in prison and three years of supervised release, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) said in a statement on Friday.
The men sought to arrange “dead drop” cash payments in exchange for information related to US national security, the statement also said.
The pair operated a “long-running”, “extensive” and “brazen” scheme to undermine US national security and support Chinese intelligence operations and recruitment in the US, Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A Eisenberg said.
According to court documents, Lai and Chen began acting as agents of China’s foreign intelligence arm, the Ministry of State Security, no later than May 2021.
Lai, who arrived in the US on a tourist visa, recruited Chen, a permanent resident, into the scheme and initially served as an intermediary between Chen and intelligence officers – until Chen was able to receive his orders directly from his handler.
In May 2022, they facilitated a secret cash payment of $10,000 from China, ordering US-based individuals to drop the cash at a specified location for collection by someone else, an arrangement known as a “dead drop”.
The two later carried out another similar operation, facilitating a payment of $20,000.
Chen and Lai also engaged in other forms of espionage, including obtaining photographs of a naval facility, military recruits, and active-duty sailors. Chen collected personal information about a US Navy employee and maintained detailed biographical information about military personnel who were potential intelligence targets.
The DOJ did not say how many times the pair had facilitated payments, nor how many people they had successfully recruited in the US.
The men were found guilty of two charges: conspiracy to act as agents of a foreign government without prior notification to the Attorney General; and acting as agents of a foreign government without prior notification.
Both pleaded guilty in court.
The pair were arrested and charged in June 2025.
In late August, US President Donald Trump said he knew China spied on the US, but “we spy on them too”.
In June, China announced that it had arrested a US citizen accused of espionage a day after US media reports said a scholar holding dual US and Myanmar citizenship was detained in early June.
The scholar, Min Zin, previously wrote opinion pieces on Myanmar politics that were critical of the military government, as well as the opposition groups it is fighting.

articles.title_orig: Shenzhen too pricey? Cost-conscious Hongkongers dig deeper into mainland China
articles.title_zh: Shenzhen too pricey? Cost-conscious Hongkongers dig deeper into mainland China
articles.content_orig:
As Hong Kong residents explore a wider range of mainland cities, businesses in Guangzhou, Zhongshan and Jiangmen are reaping rewards
Seventy-something Hong Kong retiree Leung Ching says a meal for four in Shenzhen, the megacity in mainland China roughly an hour’s train ride away, that cost just over 300 yuan (US$45) a few years ago now runs to 500 to 600 yuan.
It would cost around HK$1,000 (US$127.50) in Hong Kong, but only 300 yuan in Guangzhou and just 200 yuan in Zhongshan, two cities within two hours of Hong Kong.
“Shenzhen is becoming less and less affordable,” said Leung, a retired vendor.

articles.title_orig: China's Blue Bay initiative gets UN honor
articles.title_zh: China's Blue Bay initiative gets UN honor
articles.content_orig:
China's Blue Bay Restoration Initiative was named a 2026 United Nations World Restoration Flagship on Thursday in Yerevan, the capital of Armenia, highlighting international recognition of China's achievements in marine ecological protection and restoration.
The announcement was made at the "Restoration Day" event during the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity, or COP17.
Led by the Ministry of Natural Resources and the Ministry of Finance, the initiative is the second nationwide program from China to receive the honor, following the Shan-Shui Initiative, which was among the first global flagships in 2022. The achievement makes China the first country to have two nationwide actions recognized as World Restoration Flagships.
The World Restoration Flagship, jointly established by the United Nations Environment Programme and the Food and Agriculture Organization, is a global recognition under the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, highlighting large-scale restoration projects that are exemplary, representative and globally influential. In this round, initiatives from Colombia, Ethiopia, Italy and the United States were also honored.
At the awarding ceremony, Raimund Jehle, deputy regional representative for Europe and Central Asia at the Food and Agriculture Organization, underscored the importance of healthy coastal ecosystems for biodiversity, food security and people's livelihoods.
"Healthy coastal ecosystems support fisheries, protect communities and strengthen resilience to climate change. Their restoration requires us to work across the boundaries between land and sea and across sectors and institutions," Jehle said.
"China's Blue Bay Initiative demonstrates the value of this integrated approach, bringing together ecological restoration, coordinated governance and public investment," he added.
Building on the experience of the Yundang Lake restoration in Xiamen, Fujian province, coastal regions across China have advanced integrated land-sea management and marine ecological restoration on a large scale.
During the 13th (2016-20) and 14th Five-Year Plan periods (2021-25), China's central government allocated 36.63 billion yuan ($5.5 billion) to coastal provinces for the implementation of 194 major marine ecological restoration projects. This led to the restoration of more than 150,000 hectares of coastal wetlands, the management of Spartina alterniflora, an invasive cordgrass species, and the rehabilitation of more than 2,000 kilometers of coastline.
Zhong Chongjun, deputy director-general of the ministry's department of territorial space ecological restoration, said the recognition demonstrates full acknowledgment from the international community of China's practical achievements in marine ecological protection and restoration.
"The 194 major marine ecological restoration projects have effectively improved the quality and stability of key marine ecosystems, raised the level of biodiversity conservation, expanded quality coastal access for the public, enhanced coastal disaster prevention and mitigation capacity, and strengthened the marine ecological security barrier," Zhong said. "Thanks to sustained efforts, China's mangrove area has increased to 31,700 hectares, making the country one of the few in the world where mangrove coverage is continuously expanding," he added.
Wang Lei, director-general of the department, described the selection as both "an honor and a responsibility".
"We will take this as a new start, continuing to implement actions for blue bays, beautiful shorelines and harmonious islands," Wang said.
He emphasized the focus on improving the quality and function of key marine ecosystems, such as mangroves, coral reefs, sea grass beds, and coastal salt marshes. The goal is to deliver more ecological restoration outcomes that enhance livelihoods, boost employment and income, and foster a new development paradigm of harmony between humanity and the sea.
"We stand ready to deepen exchanges and cooperation with all countries, share our experience, build global consensus, jointly advance the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration and work hand in hand to safeguard our blue planet," Wang said.

articles.title_orig: Britain’s Prime Minister Says He’s Open to a Formal Apology for Slavery
articles.title_zh: Britain’s Prime Minister Says He’s Open to a Formal Apology for Slavery
articles.content_orig:
Financial reparations are not the answer. Working together with our Commonwealth family is the best way to ensure prosperity for us all
Andy Burnham open to calls for formal apology for Britain’s role in slave trade
O n 28 October 1787, Thomas Clarkson pushed through the crowds to reach the pulpit of Manchester Cathedral. A campaigner for abolishing slavery, he spoke urgently about the horrors of the slave trade and the humanity of enslaved people. “He drinks the cup of sorrow,” Clarkson said. “And he drinks it at our hands.”
During Black History Month , these are the stories it is important to remember. They show us the complicated truth of our history. Thousands of people in Manchester signed a petition against slavery after Clarkson’s sermon. And yet Manchester’s cotton industry was built on the labour of enslaved people. There are similar stories up and down the nation. We are a country where brave people led the way in abolishing slavery, but we are also a country that participated in the trade in human lives.
The transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people. They were denied their humanity. They were separated from their families, treated as property and worked to their deaths. I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today.
Our history is intertwined with countries that are now our allies, particularly in the Commonwealth. Next week, I will attend the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm). In an increasingly divided and dangerous world, our family of nations in the Commonwealth is vital to our interests: a beacon of stability, strength and security. Together we can face down shared challenges. We can seize opportunities for trade and economic collaboration. We can strengthen our respective countries and share our values to build a safer world for us all.
But facing a changing world together requires us to stand on firm foundations. To meet those challenges of the future, we need to face up to the past. For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery. By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function.
Having these difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future is the right thing to do. It is also the patriotic thing to do. Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.
So we are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade. Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.
Some have called for financial reparations for the slave trade. I do not believe that is the right answer. I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.
My focus is on building a future where people at home and abroad live in greater peace and prosperity.
So we will bring to the Chogm our determination to tackle the issues that affect people across our Commonwealth family and beyond.
Today, debt-servicing costs in the poorest and most vulnerable countries are at their highest in more than 25 years. More than 40% of these countries spend more on interest repayments than on health . I want to launch a new drive on debt, working with our global partners to help those countries repay over a longer time period and with better rates. That is why the chancellor, foreign secretary and I have asked Gordon Brown, who will join us at the Chogm, to help with this work.
We will also support the energy transition in the face of the climate crisis. And we will build on the incredible work being done to educate women and girls, give smaller countries a louder voice on the world stage, and end global poverty and inequality.
after newsletter promotion
I want us to build stronger relationships with each other and renew the relevance of the Commonwealth in a new era. We do that by facing our past together and focusing on a future where every person living within it has equality, security and hope.
We stand on the shoulders of those such as Thomas Clarkson and the many ordinary people who spoke out for justice and humanity.
In 1862, at the height of the American civil war, Manchester was the cotton capital of the world. In a vote at the Free Trade Hall, the humble cotton workers resolved that they would no longer handle slave-picked cotton . Their actions helped end the civil war, prompting Abraham Lincoln to write to them praising their “sublime Christian heroism”.
It is so often the case in British history that huge injustices ignored by the powers-that-be are eventually overturned by ordinary people. Those Manchester cotton workers represent that proud British tradition, and I will take inspiration from them as we go forward into our new dialogue.
Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United Kingdom

articles.title_orig: Fake US voters? China-linked accounts flood X with divisive posts ahead of midterms
articles.title_zh: Fake US voters? China-linked accounts flood X with divisive posts ahead of midterms
articles.content_orig:
Fabricated political polling has forced its way into the spotlight during the midterm election period in the United States.
Revelations that a small number of fraudulent firms have released fictitious results – some of which were picked up by news outlets and polling trackers – have raised concerns about how easily false information can acquire credibility.
Those datasets can be used to cast doubt on the electoral process. And when bad actors are unmasked, their existence can be leveraged to undermine voter confidence in election information overall.
The latest example occurred earlier this month, when Wedgewood Polls released a statement on social media admitting its statistics about a bevy of battleground states – like Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Kansas and Maine – were fake.
Wedgewood described its work as “an experimental project” designed to highlight the “vulnerabilities, lack of oversight and overall low barrier to entry” in the US polling industry.
“Having previously worked in the polling and research sector, we watched as the public’s trust in polling eroded alongside a rise in unverified, low-quality methodology,” the firm said in a statement posted to its social media account, which has now been deleted.
It justified its false data as a test to see how easy it would be for fabricated polling to gain traction among voters and the media.
“The short answer: Far too easy,” Wedgewood said.
But Wedgewood’s admission came after its surveys had already circulated through the political information ecosystem, reaching prominent media outlets like The New York Times.
The incident was the second such scandal in the 2026 election cycle, following the exposure of another operation, Median Strategies, which acknowledged in August it had also faked results as a “short-term social experiment”.
In an increasingly polarised US political environment, the incidents have roiled a polling industry – and a public – struggling to adapt to an ever-changing information landscape.
Wedgewood, which launched in June, published surveys covering competitive races across several states. Its results attracted attention from political campaigns, commentators and organisations that compile polling data.
The New York Times said its polling tracker had listed 15 Wedgewood surveys between June and October. The newspaper subsequently removed them.
In the wake of the scandal, it explained that the firm had answered questions about its personnel, methodology and funding before its results were included.
While the Times said Wedgewood’s surveys were not incorporated into the newspaper’s own presidential approval or national congressional polling averages, the case revealed a vulnerability in the process by which polling information becomes established as credible.
Polling aggregators help journalists and voters make sense of a crowded field of surveys by collecting results from multiple research organisations. Their value depends partly on their ability to distinguish reliable research from poorly conducted or fraudulent work.
Wedgewood’s success in passing some of those checks suggests that transparency on paper is not necessarily proof that research has been conducted as claimed.
According to FiftyPlusOne, a polling and forecasting website that investigated the firm, inconsistencies in the raw data and the technical identifiers associated with survey responses helped raise suspicions about its authenticity.
The investigation prompted Wedgewood to acknowledge that most of its results were fabricated.
Though Wedgewood has denied trying to mislead the public, some pollsters are not convinced, suggesting the group could was up to something more nefarious.
“We were investigating Wedgewood for faking their data,” said data journalist G Elliott Morris, who was involved in FiftyPlusOne’s probe. “They are trying to cover up for their fraud with the ‘we were doing a social experiment’ excuse.”
The consequences of fake polling extend far beyond the polling industry.
Mallory McMorrow, who ran unsuccessfully in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, has argued that a Wedgewood survey showing her support in the single digits damaged her campaign.
McMorrow said the poll left her volunteers demoralised, and journalists repeatedly contacted her to ask whether she should abandon the race.
Donations, she added, also evaporated, with Democratic supporters looking to other campaigns to invest.
In a social media post , McMorrow described the poll from Wedgewood – and another from the firm Mitchell Research and Communications – as a “one-two punch” that “killed her campaign”. She suspended her Senate bid in July.
“By that point, we took a risk and we spend our money. We put our ads up. They were working. But the damage was done. And I was drowned out by outside spending and the narrative that we had completely collapsed,” she wrote.
Experts say McMorrow’s account illustrates a broader problem: Even when a poll does not accurately measure public opinion, its findings can still influence the decisions of people who believe it does.
The Wedgewood controversy demonstrates how fraudulent data can become ammunition in an already polarised political environment.
Researchers at the University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public tracked how discussion of Wedgewood’s admission spread across social media.
Initially, much of the conversation was concentrated among polling experts and people who followed election data. But the story subsequently gained traction among influential political commentators and partisan accounts.
Some posts focused on the fact that prominent outlets and polling aggregators had listed Wedgewood’s results. Others used the revelation to question polling more broadly, particularly surveys suggesting that Democrats were competitive in closely contested races.
The researchers found the controversy became intertwined with claims that polling was systematically misleading voters or understating support for particular political parties.
“Within 24 hours, the right-wing media ecosystem had succeeded in drawing attention to the story and setting some of the most salient frames: that poll numbers around the midterms, especially poll numbers favoring Democrats, cannot be trusted,” the Center for an Informed Public wrote in its analysis.
President Donald Trump, who has regularly made false claims about US election integrity, seized on the revelations to criticise the Times for including Wedgewood’s surveys in its polling tracker.
“The New York Times got caught,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post . “Everything about The Failing New York Times is ‘ARTIFICIAL’.”
He also suggested the Wedgewood case would help his $15bn defamation suit against the Times.
“Our powerful Lawsuit against them is getting stronger and stronger everyday,” he added.
No laws exist in the US that criminalise fake polls outright.
Some advocacy groups and law scholars have argued that the publication of fake polls constitute commodities and wire fraud, warranting federal prosecution.
“Deterring this sort of fraud before it can happen – and raising awareness of it – is vital,” Tyler Yeargain wrote for the Missouri Law Review in 2020.
He argued that enforcement of election-related laws against fake pollsters has “not been fully utilized”.
“Prosecution would serve a strong federal interest,” he wrote. “The interest at stake is weightier than concerns over how fake polls can shade the accuracy of an academic endeavor in prediction markets. It is instead to deter other wrongdoers, the sort who would weaponize fake polls to manipulate elections.”
Brendan Carr, the head of the Federal Communication Commission (FCC), which regulates broadcasts in the US, said there has been “a significant surge” in fake polls during the 2026 midterms, urging networks not to amplify them. Otherwise, Carr said, they could lose their licence to operate.

articles.title_orig: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia
articles.title_zh: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia
articles.content_orig:
Marco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycott
The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.
Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.
“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”
About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.
European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.
During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as brutal and unjustified - in front of Lavrov - saying Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.
A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.
“Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”
The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.
Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.
That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.
“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.
Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.
But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.
“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.

articles.title_orig: China, Switzerland upgrade FTA
articles.title_zh: China, Switzerland upgrade FTA
articles.content_orig:
President Xi Jinping and President of the Swiss Confederation Guy Parmelin witnessed on Friday the signing of an upgraded free trade agreement, demonstrating the two countries' commitment to upholding openness and cooperation amid unilateralism and protectionism, as well as their distinctive role in promoting an open world economy.
Parmelin started a three-day working visit to China on Friday. During their talks, Xi told the Swiss leader that Switzerland is an important partner of China in Europe and has consistently been at the forefront of cooperation between China and European countries.
Switzerland was the first country on the continent of Europe to sign an FTA with China in 2013. In August this year, it became the first European country to conclude negotiations on upgrading the agreement.
Xi said that bilateral free trade cooperation reflects the two countries' political courage and their sense of responsibility in upholding open cooperation.
China is ready to work with Switzerland to uphold openness, strengthen cooperation and promote an inclusive and universally beneficial economic globalization, Xi said. The two sides should inject valuable confidence and greater certainty into China-Europe economic and trade cooperation and into global economic development, he added.
Since the establishment of diplomatic relations in 1950, China and Switzerland have pursued cooperation based on mutual benefit and a pioneering spirit, achieving tangible results and demonstrating the principles of equality, innovation and win-win cooperation, Xi said.
They have set an example for relations between countries of different sizes and with different social systems, Xi said.
This year marks the 10th anniversary of the establishment of the China-Switzerland innovative strategic partnership, which is China's first strategic partnership with a foreign country centered on innovation.
Xi called on the two sides to deepen innovation cooperation and foster collaboration in emerging industries, including the digital economy, green energy storage and artificial intelligence.
Noting Switzerland's longstanding role in China-Europe economic and trade cooperation, Xi said he hopes that Switzerland will leverage its unique influence to play a positive role in promoting the sound, balanced and steady development of China-Europe trade.
Parmelin said that Switzerland takes pride in being among the first Western countries to recognize the People's Republic of China — a decision that laid the foundation for a lasting and dynamic partnership between the two countries.
He said the swift conclusion of negotiations on upgrading the FTA reflects the high level of mutual trust between the two countries and meets the expectations of businesses and other stakeholders on both sides.
The upgraded agreement will inject fresh impetus into the development of Switzerland-China relations, Parmelin added.
Data from the customs shows that China has remained Switzerland's third-largest trading partner for 12 consecutive years. The value of bilateral trade reached approximately $65.14 billion in the first half of 2026, registering substantial growth.
In an article published on Monday by People's Daily, Qian Minjian, China's ambassador to Switzerland, said that once the upgraded China-Switzerland FTA takes effect, over 99 percent of goods exported by one country to the other will be duty-free, while market access will be further expanded in the areas of trade in services and investment.
Feng Zhongping, a senior research fellow at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' Institute of European Studies, said the upgrading of the China-Switzerland FTA comes at a critical time when economic and trade relations between China and the European Union are facing considerable uncertainty, with trade frictions continuing to weigh on bilateral ties.
The upgraded FTA demonstrates the potential for China and European countries to achieve mutual benefit and shared development through cooperation, he added.

articles.title_orig: Samsung mercilessly mocks iPhone Duo ‘crackgate’ in Galaxy Z Fold 8 ads [Video]
articles.title_zh: Samsung mercilessly mocks iPhone Duo ‘crackgate’ in Galaxy Z Fold 8 ads [Video]
articles.content_orig:
Samsung isn’t holding back when it comes to the iPhone Duo’s messy start. In new ads, the company mocks iPhone Duo’s “crackgate” with a push for customers to buy the Galaxy Z Fold 8 instead, and there’s not an ounce of subtlety here.
Following the debut of Apple’s first foldable, an unfortunate trend has emerged among early buyers. A number of users found that their display “cracked” with the display panel dying in the center, all in the exact same way, implying there’s a flaw within Apple’s hinge design.
Apple is replacing affected devices , but it is a somewhat harrowing reminder that this is the company’s first attempt at this hardware.
And Samsung is happy to point that out.
In an ad for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 on Instagram , Samsung says that “folding is nothing new to us” and that “we know a thing or eight.” It cuts right to the chase: “Switch to Galaxy Z Fold8.” The attached imagery then depicts the iPhone Duo’s well-known screen “crack.
That one was posted to Samsung Canada’s account, while another ad from Samsung Malaysia further takes that up a notch:
Feeling a little FOMO seeing all this talk about durability… oops, we’ve just been busy folding and getting on with our day
Samsung Australia similarly poked fun at Apple’s durability woes with a post about “how life sounds when your screen doesn’t break when opening your phone.”
Another post from Samsung Saudi Arabia puts the iPhone Duo crack on a Galaxy Z Fold 8 before revealing it’s just a wallpaper.

articles.title_orig: Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack
articles.title_zh: Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack
articles.content_orig:
Two major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group as the likely culprits in the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.
The Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking unit also known as TraderTraitor, was identified "with high confidence" by TRM Labs, as well as Chainalysis.
This incident is just the latest linked to the country, one of the poorest in the world and where access to the internet is severely restricted.
Experts accuse the government of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of relying on cybercrime to finance itself, something Pyongyang has long denied.
Though not financial, the nation's most spectacular suspected hack took place in 2014. The target: Sony Pictures, which had made the Hollywood film The Interview. The film involves a plot to assassinate Kim.
The resulting hack exposed thousands of embarrassing emails exchanged among the studio's top executives.
Last year, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said North Korea was responsible for the theft of $1.5bn on the Bybit exchange.
In the aftermath of that incident, the agency said TraderTraitor had moved to quickly launder and disperse the stolen assets, converting them to Bitcoin and other digital assets with a goal of eventually turning them into hard currency.
The FBI has broadly accused North Korea of "illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities".
The nation has systematically developed its cyber operations, recruiting the most promising students from universities and channeling them into hacker groups overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, according to reports.
Some of the cyberwarfare conducted takes place just over the nation's border in China, according to analysis from tech groups.
Much of its hacking activity has centred on monetary gain.
North Korean hackers are also suspected in the theft of $620m worth of cryptocurrency in 2022.
In this most recent heist, North Korean agents are accused of using a special authorisation to turn a Binance hot wallet, which is connected to the internet, into one that moved funds automatically to the attacker.
TRM said it's likely the attacker gained access to Binance's hot wallet signing system as part of the scheme.
Binance  has not directly responded to the BBC's queries about the incident's potential links to the area.
The company had initially said it thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.
"Our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said.
Some 80% of stolen assets have been secured, a Binance spokesperson said on Friday, but the rest remains unaccounted for.
If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become – a sign that the tools of the hacking trade have grown sharper.
Experts say the rise of artificial intelligence has also given threat actors new ways to carry out crime, through automation and other means.
In this case, it's plausible that AI was used to infiltrate Binance's systems.
As Chainalysis put it, the attacker used laundering patterns "we have not seen before".

articles.title_orig: McDonald's dealt legal setback as judge allows McRib meat lawsuit to proceed
articles.title_zh: McDonald's dealt legal setback as judge allows McRib meat lawsuit to proceed
articles.content_orig:
A 'Barron's Roundtable' panel discusses how the fast-food chain will manage the pinch on consumers' wallets.
A federal judge ruled Friday that McDonald's must face a proposed class action lawsuit accusing the fast-food giant of misleading customers about the meat used in its popular McRib sandwich.
U.S. District Judge April Perry in Chicago rejected the company's bid to dismiss the lawsuit in its entirety, allowing consumer deception, fraud and unjust enrichment claims to proceed while dismissing five other claims without prejudice.
The lawsuit, filed by four consumers in December, alleges that McDonald's designed the McRib patty to resemble a rack of pork ribs despite containing no actual rib meat.
The plaintiffs argue that the sandwich's name, appearance and marketing mislead customers into believing they are purchasing a more expensive cut of pork.
MCDONALD'S HIT WITH LAWSUIT CLAIMING MCRIB CONTAINS NO REAL RIB MEAT
McDonald's must face a proposed class action lawsuit accusing the fast-food giant of misleading customers about the meat used in its popular McRib sandwich. (David Paul Morris/Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
Perry determined that it was too early to conclude that consumers could not reasonably expect the sandwich to contain rib meat, citing allegations about its marketing and consumer surveys submitted by the plaintiffs.
One survey found that 72% of respondents expected the McRib to contain rib meat, while another found that 67% considered rib meat important or very important to their purchasing decision, according to the court filing.
The ruling allows portions of the case to proceed but does not establish that McDonald's engaged in deceptive advertising.
NELSON PELTZ-LED GROUP OFFERS TO BUY WENDY’S FOR $1.4B
There are nearly 45,000 McDonald's restaurants worldwide. (Edgar Su/Reuters, File / Reuters Photos)
As FOX Business previously reported , the lawsuit alleges that the McRib contains lower-grade pork products, including pork shoulder, heart, tripe and stomach, rather than rib meat.
McDonald's has denied the allegations, maintaining that the sandwich contains 100% pork sourced from U.S. farmers and suppliers. The company previously told FOX Business that it does not use heart, tripe or scalded stomach in the McRib patty.
McDonald's argued that the sandwich's name does not mislead reasonable consumers and that its publicly available ingredient list identifies pork as the primary ingredient.
Perry rejected the argument that the McRib's trademarked name shields the company from deceptive marketing claims, noting that other McDonald's products, including the McChicken and Egg McMuffin, have names that describe their ingredients.
GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO BY CLICKING HERE
A representative for McDonald's did not immediately respond to FOX Business' request for comment.
Introduced in 1981, the McRib has developed a loyal following through its periodic limited-time returns to McDonald's menus. The sandwich features a boneless pork patty covered in barbecue sauce and topped with onions and pickles.
There are nearly 14,000 McDonald's restaurants in the U.S. and more than 45,000 worldwide.

articles.title_orig: Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue
articles.title_zh: Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue
articles.content_orig:
In Armenia's capital this week a fight between politicians broke out - not the mass brawl in its parliament that was so widely documented on social media - but between delegates from nearly 200 countries.
The world's nations have been gathered in Yerevan for nearly two weeks  negotiating, and arguing, over a new agreement on nature.
Early on Saturday morning, hours after talks were due to finish, they finally agreed the key parts of a new action plan.
"And that's it. Perfect," said the meeting president, Hambardzum Matevosyan.
Four years earlier the same countries had signed a landmark deal committing to "halt and reverse" the decline of nature.
That global deal in 2022 - the Global Biodiversity Framework - contained 24 targets including putting 30% of the world's land and seas into protection by the end of the decade.
They agreed that action was urgent.
The world is currently in a sixth mass extinction event with species becoming extinct at 100 times the natural rate because of human activities, scientists say.
But according to the UN this week, the world is on track to achieve just one of those two dozen targets.
As part of this week's deal, countries acknowledged they were falling behind.
"While not particularly exciting or detailed, it's good news that countries could reach agreement," said Catherine Weller, from environmental charity Fauna & Flora.
"We cannot just plod on to 2030 without a course correction; nature is critical to all life on Earth: to our economies, to our wellbeing," she added.
This was echoed by Craig Bennett, CEO of The Wildlife Trusts, who told BBC News: "We are still seeing an appalling loss, threatening the collapse of ecosystems globally. We run out of words really about how serious this is."
But he added "the better news is there are so many examples worldwide about how... to turn things around".
Countries have put 623 million acres (252m hectares) of degraded land into protection - an area bigger than Greenland.
Just last month the WWF praised conservation efforts which had achieved the recovery of key species including elephants, green sea turtles and tigers.
Countries have recognised the main barrier to accelerating those efforts is money.
In 2022, they agreed they would put $30bn (£22.4bn) towards nature recovery efforts by the end of the decade, and mobilise a further $170bn from private sources.
But years later many nations have been redirecting international aid to defence budgets and to deal with repeated energy shocks, such that pledges are not at the rate required to reach those targets, according to the UN.
At this meeting, more than $1bn was pledged, with half of that coming from philanthropists including Leonardo DiCaprio's Re:wild organisation.
Anna Ducros, a researcher at the International Institute for Environment and Development, said there had been some progress on countries committing to reducing subsidies for industries harmful to the environment.
"A concrete example is that governments subsidise large-scale fishing that is especially harmful for nature - for example, trawling."
Ducros, who was in attendance at the talks, added: "Right now, we have the situation where governments are paying twice.
"So they know that they need to increase spending on nature and climate, but at the same time, they're damaging nature."
A specific funding pot, the Cali Fund, was previously set up for private companies that profit from using genetic material found in the environment to donate to. It was estimated up to $3.6bn could be raised annually -  at the start of the meeting just $10,000 had been pledged.
Little progress was made on that issue - its voluntary nature makes it difficult to put pressure on companies, Bennett acknowledged.
"When you have countries that have rich biodiversity in them and you have companies trying to make money out of the genetic material found in those countries they should be paying those communities," he said. "That should not be controversial."
One of the easier issues on the agenda was meant to be the approval of scientific reports into the state of nature.
But a small group of countries, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, were reported to have frustrated that process.
"The attacks on science have bothered me a lot," French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut was reported as saying by the AFP news agency.
Next month countries will gather for the annual climate conference - COP31. Its own science body, the IPCC, has faced similar challenges in the past month with passing its own scientific reports and securing funding.
"This is such a blatant political move...and the IPCC is no such place for such political manoeuvring since the outputs are in humanity's interest," said Prof David Lee, from Manchester University, who has worked on previous reports.

articles.title_orig: What to know about the $6.3B hack on Binance, likely the biggest-ever crypto theft
articles.title_zh: What to know about the $6.3B hack on Binance, likely the biggest-ever crypto theft
articles.content_orig:
This live page has now closed, you can read more in our news story here
The US Secret Service says it is "working around the clock" with partners to help track funds stolen from cryptocurrency exchange Binance
The $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) hack is thought to be the largest of its kind in history - our cyber correspondent breaks down what we know
Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, says it has "begun recovering" some funds and believes there was more than one hacker involved in the "complex attack"
I've got a Binance account - can I check if I've been affected?
Analysts suspect North Korea could be behind it - one analysis firm says it has observed funds from this hack "commingling" with funds from another that has widely been attributed to North Korean actors
The regime has repeatedly been accused of using cryptocurrency theft to generate revenue to help fund its weapons programmes, our Japan correspondent writes
Here's a guide to some of the key terms used around cryptocurrencies
Edited by Craig Hoyle, with cyber correspondent Joe Tidy and technology reporters Liv McMahon and Laura Cress
The US Secret Service says its investigators are working "around the clock" to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds stolen in what is thought to be the largest hack in history - worth up to $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn).
The affected firm Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange, which earlier said it had "begun recovering" some funds after yesterday's attack.
Binance co-CEO Richard Tend said the hack attacked the firm's own hot wallet by abusing something called "multi-signature protocol EIP-7702".
This meant the thieves were able to bypass the usual methods of verification used by the platform - most of the money left Binance wallets in about 20 minutes , one expert told the BBC.
This did not involve just one person, and the hacker used a "self-destruct mechanism" to destroy tooling and traces as it went, Teng said.
Analysts suspect that North Korea could be behind the attack, with many pointing to the hacking unit TraderTraitor.
Why North Korea? Crypto theft is a big money-maker for the regime, our Japan correspondent writes.
Investigators are still looking into the attack, aiming to freeze assets and trace the hackers, while the US Federal Bureau of Investigation has said it is "aware of the incident" .
Teng earlier said that Binance will share a full proof-of-reserves report by Monday and an initial view hopefully before that.
Withdrawal services remain switched off until they pass "rigorous testing", which Teng earlier said is "on track" to be completed within 40 hours .
If you are a Binance customer, our technology reporter Laura Cress explains how to check your accounts .
We are ending our live coverage now but you can read more in our story here .
Joe Tidy Cyber correspondent
This is a really troubling time for the cryptocurrency world.
Every year we are seeing  enormous hacks of this kind of magnitude.
Last year $1.5bn (Â£1.12bn) was taken from Bybit.
Before that it was $600m (Â£433m) from Poly Network in 2021 and $540m (Â£412m) from Ronin in 2022.
As well as these hacks, which are a worry for industry titans like Binance and other cryptocurrency exchanges and companies, this is all a troubling time for individuals.
We have seen an increase in digital theft of cryptocurrency and attacks when people are being physically intimidated to hand over the private keys to their crypto wallets.
The value of cryptocurrency is such now that it is worth criminals going after people individually.
Mackenzie Jackson, from cybersecurity firm Aikido, tells the BBC that developer devices are attacked every day.
He says hackers have shifted from going after company infrastructure to going after the machines of the people who run it. Those machines hold the digital keys that unlock a companyâs systems, so an attacker can act as that engineer.
Jackson says techniques vary, but include tricking workers into installing malware under the pretext of a job interview, or interfering with code that developers rely on.
"Binance says this was a more complex process than a single click, which points to a chain," he explains.
"From one laptop, an attacker can open one internal system, then another, until they reach a service trusted to send out withdrawals. Those withdrawals travel through a legitimate route, so they can look routine.â
We don't yet know who was behind the attack, but as our cyber correspondent Joe Tidy says, all fingers are pointing towards North Korea.
There are two main reasons for this: investigators including the FBI have blamed North Korea for similar hacks in the past, and crypto analytics firms say this hack looks like previous hacks widely attributed to North Korea.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists," says Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs.
It says it has "high confidence" that North Korean group TraderTraitor - also known as the Lazarus group - is responsible.
Chainalysis, another crypto analytics firm, also says it has a "high degree of confidence" that North Korea was behind the hack.
It says it observed funds stolen from Binance "commingling" with funds stolen from another hack of a different crypto exchange last month which was also widely attributed to North Korean actors.
North Korea has always denied it is behind such hacking, but Tidy says "the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling".
Binance has not responded to the BBCâs queries about possible links to North Korea.
After we heard from the FBI earlier, another US government agency has commented on the hack.
The US Secret Service, which is the lead federal agency for financial crimes and protecting the US financial system, says it's "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.
The agency goes on to say that it's "coordinating closely with the United States Attorneyâs Office for the District of Columbia and law enforcement partners to identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice".
"Our investigation remains in its early stages, and we will provide additional information as appropriate.â
Kurumi Mori Japan correspondent
Bitcoin's value (BTC) fell after the news of the Binance hack, with its price dropping by about four percentage points.
But we should note that in the early days of crypto, BTC could lose 20% or 30% of its value in a single day after a cryptocurrency theft. So that's likely a sign that the crypto market has since matured.
And when you look at the bigger picture, there are trillions of dollars in crypto today, so losing this amount of $6.3 billion doesnât seem to be the end of the road for digital currencies.
Still, Binance has called this a âcomplex attackâ and we're yet to see how this will all play out.
Tara Mewawalla Live reporter
Ari Redbord, chief policy officer of the crypto analytics
company TRM Labs, tells the BBC what stands out in this incident is the speed of the
theft.
Binance earlier said its initial investigation suggests the security incident may have involved a "compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" which allowed the hackers to gain access and submit unauthorised transactions.
Most of the $6.36bn left Binance wallets in about 20 minutes, Redbord says, starting at 20:05 GMT on Thursday.
"That
speed is the product of long preparation," he says.
He explains that an "operator wallet" was funded 36 hours earlier by the hacker, and was most likely used to make transactions which allowed the hacker to gain access to the authorisation system.
The "signatures" to authorise those transactions would have been prepared in advance, Redbord adds.
Joe Tidy Cyber correspondent
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng has posted a video on social media outlining the latest in the investigation into how the hack happened.

articles.title_orig: World trekker Karl Bushby's final push home to Hull
articles.title_zh: World trekker Karl Bushby's final push home to Hull
articles.content_orig:
With his journey almost complete, Karl Bushby reflects on adventures that have taken him across four continents, as well as strained relationships and how life as he knows it is about to change dramatically.
Back in 1998, the former paratrooper, then aged 29, set off from Punta Arenas, Chile, to walk an unbroken path to his home city of Hull, without breaking two self-imposed rules: not to return to the UK until he had completed his journey, and not to use transport to advance.
Now 57, he is embarking on his final few miles having hacked his way through the jungles of the Darién Gap , crossed the frozen Bering Strait and, just a few weeks ago, swum the English Channel .
At the end, he will be met by his 36-year-old son Adam, a 12-year-old granddaughter whom he has never met, his father and brothers. His mother will be waiting at his childhood home that he left 28 years ago.
"We're definitely in terra incognita [unknown territory] right now, or pretty soon will be," says Bushby, as I join him in rural Lincolnshire.
"Right now, I'm comfortable because I'm doing what I do, but pretty soon that's going to screech to a halt."
A bit like "The Beast", Bushby's heavy duty hardcart.
Just a couple of miles into this leg, Bushby's handcart, which he uses to carry essential supplies, sustains a puncture.
"We haven't had one of these for a long time," he says. "This could be a pain. Damn."
As I watched him attempt a hasty roadside repair, he flashed a grin before adding: "If it was raining, I'd probably be moaning a bit more."
"The first few days that I was in Dover, it started raining. But we'd managed to just thread the needle as far as the weather was concerned. We had those perfect three days [for the swim]."
Bushby quips: "You guys know you drive on the wrong side of the road, right?"
His use of the word "you" speaks of his disconnection from home.
Bushby is well versed in overcoming physical barriers, such as a flat tyre.
But is he prepared for what is to follow?
"Everything that I am and everything that I know of me is going to go away," he says. "And that's going to be a problem. You're going to have the old identity crisis, because Karl is this [an adventurer] and has been for half his life.
"I will have to figure out who I am again. What is the meaning to it all? How do I find that meaning and purpose? How do I fill that hole I'm suddenly going to find myself in?
"Every fibre of my being, every day, has been what I'm doing right now. It has been the mission.
"I think the old adage goes... the only thing worse than a man who can't fulfil his dreams is a man who's fulfilled his dreams... because then what?"
Angela Maxwell, an American long-distance walker, joined him for the walk from Dover, where he landed after swimming the Channel.
"I think Karl might be surprised how much he'll miss the road," she says. "We joke sometimes that Karl doesn't love walking. But he loves the mission. He loves the passion, the purpose."
Bushby has been surprised by the interest his return to the UK has stoked.
"It's been almost overwhelming. The amount of people that have recognised me along the way. It's cool. It gets a bit weird at times when people get really, really excited, and I just can't work out why. From my perspective, it just seems a little strange.
"I'm some guy who's just walking."
A car pulls into a lay-by and the driver asks if he is the Karl Bushby. The men pose for a selfie.
Bushby has consistently denied this is a spiritual undertaking; a journey of discovery.
But does he think the global interest in his story stems from an inner wanderlust present in many of us, but acted upon by few?
"I think that's it," he says.
"I've lived a million men's dreams. A lot of people would love to walk away from home and just keep going."
Bushby says his "opportunity to walk" came following the end of his marriage, with his wife returning to Northern Ireland with their son.
The reality of life on the road is not as rosy as it might first appear, it seems.
"I'm dealing with the day-to-day stuff - punctures, just trying to find a place where you can wash your underwear. That's my life. That's the mundane stuff, walking in the rain, it's never-ending kilometres.
"It's not as glorious as it looks."
Bushby says he has only spent about 15 of the 28 years walking, often retreating to Mexico, where costs are low, between stints.
The remainder of the time has been spent applying for visas and "dealing with geopolitics", he says.
Travel restrictions during the Covid-19 pandemic also resulted in delays.
Under the rules he set for his journey, Bushby could not return to the UK to meet his family.
On rare occasions, he met his son and parents, who are divorced, in other countries.
"Family is family, right?" says Bushby.
"They're always going to be there. But there will be strain. There will be distance. So much so that you've grown apart to some degree. You don't really know each other anymore.
"As far as a love life goes, standby. You're going to take a kick in the nuts. It's not going to work out for you."
Soon after arriving in Dover, he tasted fish, chips and mushy peas for the first time in almost three decades.
He said nowhere else in the world does the dish quite like the Brits.
But venturing beyond the superficial, he appears not to have missed the UK.
"I've had the whole world to play with, so I've been distracted by many shiny things."
Bushby believes he has not aged conventionally.
"I'm older, but I don't feel that old. I still feel way too young for my age, mentally. I still identify with that guy from the Americas way back when."
With a twinkle in his eye, he adds: "I have still got that sense of adventure."
His journey has also enabled him to meet many people.
"I personally have met the very best of humanity, and that's been a very uplifting thing. It's reaffirmed my belief and faith in humanity. The kindness of strangers made it all come together.
"I couldn't have done it without the world."
Before sponsors and a book deal, Bushby claims he was a "penniless backpacker" who relied on donations and even food discarded on roadsides to survive.
He has advice for others pondering an adventure.
"Take any given opportunity. You can do a lot more than you ever imagined. A little bit of self-confidence will take you an awful long way. You're not going to achieve anything by not doing anything."
What advice would he give to a young Bushby about to set off for Chile?
"He doesn't want to hear it. You don't tell him anything. Just grin at him and let him be."

articles.title_orig: Italy’s PM deploys troops as nation faces widespread strikes and port blockades
articles.title_zh: Italy’s PM deploys troops as nation faces widespread strikes and port blockades
articles.content_orig:
ROME — Tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Rome, Milan and other Italian cities Friday as part of nationwide demonstrations against the cost of living and high military spending.
The demonstrations were largely peaceful but an NBC News crew saw police use a water cannon on protesters and groups of police charging to disperse protesters in Rome on Friday night.
After several weeks of violent protests in Italy and throughout Europe , more widespread disruption is expected after the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) and other trade unions called on workers in both the public and private sectors to strike and protest.
The demonstrations in Italy appear to have been partly inspired by those in France , where some of the worst rioting in decades erupted in cities across the country after student protests about the state of education in the country evolved into wider actions about the cost of living and social security.
Elsewhere in Europe, a huge encampment of tents has occupied a square in Madrid since late last month, and thousands of people in Portugal have taken to the streets in the city of Lisbon. Tear gas and water cannons were also used on black-clad protesters in Brussels.
In Rome, many waved communist and Palestinian flags, as well as signs against the Iran war. Some let off pink smoke bombs. There was a jovial mood among the demonstrators as they lined up before the march, as has often been the case early on at previous protests, only for violence to break out later.
Protesters storm the Colosseum in Rome
Giovanna Di Matteo, a member of the left-wing Potere al Popolo! party, said she was protesting against the government that “did nothing for the people of this country.”
The government had spent money on the military “while they cut on welfare, they cut on services and people cannot reach the end of the month,” she said. “They have no money for their houses, they have no money for gasoline and everything.”
Luca, a 20-year-old medical student said the protesters felt they were “still not being heard, that everything is still the same,” and the government didn’t “care about our voice, about our voices, and about the future of this nation that is our nation.”
“We have been completely screwed by the fact that the wages do not keep up on inflation and the wages in general do not keep up with the cost of living,” added Luca, who asked to have his last name withheld out of fear of repercussions from law enforcement.
Major demonstrations also took place in other cities and towns across Italy.
They came after a number of protests in recent weeks have turned violent. Groups of masked protesters looted stores in Milan and elsewhere and threw projectiles at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons earlier this month.
Italian police were out in force again Friday with riot brigades, drones and helicopters visible in the skies above the Rome protest.
Their presence was heavy after protesters stormed Rome’s historic Colosseum on Saturday, while in the south, farmers and truckers have blockaded highways and ports to protest high fuel prices which have risen since the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni , who has made law and order a key tenet of her administration, said she had “great respect” for peaceful protesters on X earlier this month.
But her right-wing government has since introduced tougher penalties for rioters, including financial liability for parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.
“There is nothing revolutionary about vandalizing and stealing. Vandalism and theft are not protest, they are criminality,” Meloni said on social media after unveiling the legislation.
The government also said it would deploy 500 army troops alongside the police in Milan until the end of the year.
NBC News Chief Foreign Correspondent
Sara Monetta is a multimedia producer based in London.

articles.title_orig: Trump says Iran wants to talk, predicts conflict will end 'very soon'
articles.title_zh: Trump says Iran wants to talk, predicts conflict will end 'very soon'
articles.content_orig:
Coverage for this event has ended.
A supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of oil caught fire Friday after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said, according to state media.
It was the fourth oil tanker to suffer an explosion Friday after using unauthorized routes through the strait, the Guard said, according to The Associated Press.
Tehran has repeatedly said vessels must receive permission before traveling through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran warned last month that vessels traveling through the strait without permission risked "destruction."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Friday with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud to discuss regional issues, including Iran, Sudan and Yemen, the State Department said.
They met on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta.
"They discussed bilateral cooperation on a number of regional issues, including in Iran, Sudan, and Yemen," the State Department said in a statement.
"Secretary Rubio also signed the Expo 2030 participation contract, formalizing U.S. participation in Expo 2030 Riyadh, where we will showcase American innovation, expand opportunities for U.S. businesses, and strengthen our partnership with Saudi Arabia," the statement added.
Iran's political establishment is showing signs of divisions over how to end the country's prolonged conflict with the U.S. and Israel as diplomatic efforts intensify, according to Iran International .
Reformist and moderate figures have pushed for renewed negotiations with Washington, while conservatives and hardliners have emphasized military deterrence and maintaining Tehran's demands, the outlet reported.
The debate follows a reported call from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to end the war, while maintaining that any agreement must meet Iran's conditions, according to Iran International.
President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for negotiations, arguing that prolonged uncertainty is hurting Iran's economy.
Hardliners, meanwhile, have argued that Tehran should strengthen its military position and economic resilience.
Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Friday that President Donald Trump has been "very upfront" with Americans about the impact the war with Iran is having on fuel prices , calling the increase a "short-term consequence."
"If you also look at what the president has done for our energy industry, he is bringing down the price of gasoline and diesel," Leavitt said during an appearance on "The Story with Martha MacCallum."
"Of course, he's been very upfront with voters in Iowa and all across the country about what the war in Iran is doing," she said. "It's a short-term consequence. But overall, his energy policy will bring gas prices and diesel costs down again."
Leavitt contrasted Trump's energy agenda with Democrats' policies.
"If you look at it in contrast to what the Democrats want to do, they want to completely shut down and phase out our country from fossil fuels, which will jack up energy costs, which will not be good for anyone in rural America or anywhere in America," she said.
Yemen's government said Friday that Iran-aligned Houthis launched ballistic missile attacks targeting Aden International Airport and the presidential palace complex in the city.
A spokesperson for Yemen's armed forces said the Houthis targeted the airport and the Maashiq presidential palace complex, according to Reuters.
Officials did not immediately provide details on casualties or damage, or say whether the missiles struck their intended targets.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Streamer Hasan Piker compared pro-Israel Jewish voters in Michigan to the Ku Klux Klan during a livestream Thursday.
Piker made the comparison while discussing campaign volunteers for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed canvassing a Jewish neighborhood outside Detroit.
He called it "the wildest door-knocking operation of all time," saying volunteers were trying to convince "one of the more Zionist, wealthy districts in the country to vote for a Muslim anti-Zionist."
"Brave soldiers — all of 'em," Piker said.
“This is the equivalent of going to that, like, Klan, KKK neighborhood to stump for like a Black candidate,” he said. “... The supremacist attitude underlying in their worldview is identical.”
He added, “If you are pro-Israel to the degree that you are making a big fuss about never voting for Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim anti-Zionist, yes, it is the equivalent. ... It’s racial supremacy. It’s Jewish supremacy.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned Friday that ongoing global crises threaten energy and food supplies, trade and freedom of navigation as G20 foreign ministers gathered in Atlanta.
"We are tasked, on behalf of the nations that we serve, to work together with one another to coordinate responses to emerging crises and to protect our shared interests," Rubio said in opening remarks, according to Reuters.
"We can help set the context for expanded geopolitical stability and the broader economic prosperity agenda that our leaders will tackle."
The meeting comes as the ongoing war with Iran has raised concerns about global energy supplies and shipping.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Germany's Foreign Office said Friday that most G20 nations agree that Iran must return to negotiations.
"Most of the [G20] share our view: [Iran] must come to the negotiating table, the [Houthis] must cease their attacks, and [Russia] must stop driving global [food security] towards collapse with its attacks in the Black Sea," the account wrote on X.
The statement came as G20 nations gathered amid heightened tensions in the Middle East.
President Donald Trump said Friday that Iran wants "to talk" as the war stretches into its eighth month.
"They want to talk. They keep talking," Trump told reporters.
The president claimed that Iran is struggling to pay its security forces as the conflict continues.
"Look, they're not paying their soldiers, they're not paying their police. They're, you know, they're in a lot of trouble," he said.
The president also described the conflict as "not a typical war" and said Washington is spending "very little money, relatively speaking."
Trump also defended the cost of the U.S. campaign, saying the money was spent "in order to get rid of a nuclear weapon," while arguing U.S. actions in Venezuela have more than offset the expense.
"Any money we've spent in Iran, we've more than made up for with what we did in Venezuela," he said.
The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh on Friday again warned Americans in Saudi Arabia to exercise extreme caution around airports amid ongoing Houthi attacks and travel disruptions.
In its latest security alert, the embassy reiterated that non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members were ordered to leave Saudi Arabia effective Oct. 23 due to "safety risks."
"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions. The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area," the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh wrote on X.
U.S. citizens were also warned of potential attacks on airports, airspace closures, flight cancellations and other travel disruptions.
"Please take extreme caution if you choose to use airports in Saudi Arabia," the post added.
October saw the highest number of reported maritime incidents in the Strait of Hormuz region since the U.S.-Iran conflict began , according to data released by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
The UKMTO report shows incidents across the Strait of Hormuz, Arabian Gulf and Gulf of Oman climbed to their highest monthly level in October, with 144 total events reported since Feb. 28.
